transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Good morning. My name is Katie, and I will be your conference facilitator today. Welcome to Chevron's Second Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded. I will now turn the conference call over to Head of Investor Relations of Chevron Corporation, Jeanine Wai. Please go ahead.

transcript.speaker: Jeanine Wai
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: Thank you, Katie. Welcome to Chevron's Second Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call and Webcast. I'm Jeanine Wai, Head of Investor Relations. Our Chairman and CEO, Mike Wirth; CFO, Eimear Bonner; and President, New Energy, Jeff Gustavson, are on the call with me today. We'll refer to the slides and prepared remarks that are available on Chevron's website. Before we begin, please be reminded that this presentation contains estimates, projections and other forward-looking statements. A reconciliation of non-GAAP measures can be found in the appendix of this presentation. Please review the cautionary statement and additional information presented on Slide 2. Now I'll turn it over to Mike.

transcript.speaker: Michael Wirth
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Thanks, Jeanine. Amid geopolitical uncertainty and market volatility, Chevron delivered a strong second quarter, driven by our consistent strategy, capital discipline and strong execution. Global upstream production grew more than 5% quarter-over-quarter, underpinned by exceptional reliability across key assets. In the U.S., we achieved a new upstream production record of nearly 2.1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day and record refinery throughput of over 1 million barrels per day. At the same time, we maintained financial and capital discipline, achieving our structural cost reduction target six months early, with $3 billion of annual run rate savings since 2024. Hess synergy benefits have also been delivered six months early. We continue to capture strong capital efficiencies in U.S. shale and tight, and expect to spend 25% less CapEx per barrel of oil equivalent in 2026 compared to last year. And we strengthened our balance sheet to underpin long-term investments to deliver the reliable energy the world will need for decades to come. This month also marks the one-year anniversary of the Hess acquisition. We pulled value forward, capturing 50% more synergies than initially targeted, with $1.5 billion realized six months ahead of schedule. The Hess assets are generating strong free cash flow, which has been roughly double the incremental dividends and accretive to shareholders on a per share basis. This reflects the quality of the combined portfolio. Guyana is a world-class asset with significant resource depth that is expected to extend high-margin oil growth into the 2030s. In the Bakken, we're leveraging best practices from our shale and tight business to drive performance improvement, drilling laterals that are on average 28% longer, optimizing workovers and applying advanced chemicals. And we're also maintaining similar production with one less rig. Further, we're benefiting from the talented Hess employees who bring deep expertise in offshore, unconventional and exploration. The entire organization is stronger because of this combination. I'll now hand it over to Jeff, who will share an update on power.

transcript.speaker: Jeff Gustavson
transcript.title: President, New Energy
transcript.content: Thanks, Mike. The U.S. is undergoing a structural shift in electricity demand as AI accelerates, and reliable power is becoming the critical constraint. Chevron is well positioned to address this challenge. We bring a combination of assets and capabilities we believe few can match: a leading U.S. natural gas portfolio, extensive experience with large-scale behind-the-meter power, proven project execution capabilities, and strong partnerships that provide access to critical equipment and leading customers. This reflects Chevron's strategy in action. We're leveraging advantaged assets, customer relationships, execution capabilities and partnerships to deliver reliable, affordable energy while creating long-term shareholder value. While many data center power projects have been announced, few have secured long-term customer commitments for behind-the-meter power and only one is at multi-gigawatt scale, Project Kilby. This demonstrates our ability to execute at speed and scale. We recently signed a 20-year take-or-pay power purchase agreement with Microsoft for 2.67 gigawatts of firm behind-the-meter capacity, supporting its co-located data center complex. We're now focused on execution, with permitting and EPC activities progressing towards a final investment decision later this year. Kilby is expected to deliver mid-teens returns and long-duration contracted cash flows that are independent of commodity price cycles. Importantly, Kilby provides a repeatable model. We're already in advanced discussions on additional opportunities with existing and potential customers for future projects. We've engaged closely with local stakeholders throughout development and have been encouraged by the strong support we've received in West Texas. I'll now turn it over to Eimear to discuss the financial results.

transcript.speaker: Eimear Bonner
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Thanks, Jeff. For the second quarter, Chevron reported earnings of $12.1 billion or $6.11 per share. Adjusted earnings were $12 billion or $6.06 per share. Cash flow from operations, excluding working capital, was nearly $20 billion. Organic CapEx was $4.4 billion for the quarter. We now expect to finish the year at the lower end of our guidance range of $18 billion to $19 billion. And our net debt coverage ratio improved, reflecting strong cash generation in the quarter. Adjusted second quarter earnings were $9.2 billion higher versus last quarter. Adjusted upstream earnings increased due to higher realizations, higher liftings and favorable timing effects and were partly offset by higher DD&A and tax-related expenses. Adjusted downstream earnings increased primarily due to higher refining margins and favorable timing effects. Chevron generated $19.7 billion of cash flow from operations, excluding working capital, and $15.4 billion of adjusted free cash flow in the quarter. We reduced debt by more than $8 billion, further strengthening our balance sheet and financial flexibility. Net debt to CFFO at the end of the second quarter was 0.6x. Following the large build in the first quarter, working capital unwound by $2.9 billion as commodity prices decreased through the quarter. On production, we had our second highest quarter ever, maintaining strong operating momentum across all our key assets and growing production by over 200,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. Reliable operations defined the quarter. In the U.S., we achieved records for total production, Permian production and throughput at multiple facilities in the Gulf of America. International production was also strong at nearly 2 million barrels of oil equivalent per day. And TCO and Australia operated at or near full rates and the impact from the Middle East conflict remained isolated to the Partitioned Zone, representing about 1% of second quarter total production. Costs always matter, and they always will. We achieved $3 billion of structural cost reductions over the past 12 months, reaching our target six months ahead of schedule. Thanks to the hard work and relentless focus across the organization, more than 70% of the savings came from efficiency gains, underscoring the quality of the improvements delivered. Through these reductions, we have largely offset inflationary effects while we continued to grow across key assets like the Permian, Gulf of America and Guyana. We're never satisfied and never done. And we will continue to look for ways to lower costs to drive lasting value. Our plan is clear: execute safely and reliably, deliver on our objectives and continue to expand our opportunity set for the future. Our second quarter performance demonstrates strong execution and results that can be seen in our bottom line. We remain confident in the 2030 objectives we outlined last November, including annual production growth of 2% to 3%, adjusted free cash flow growth averaging greater than 10% per year and more than 3% improvement on return on capital employed, all at flat commodity prices that are lower than today. We also continue to develop robust growth options for the next decade, building new resource options across regions and asset classes. Achieving the power milestone, stacking multiple exploration successes and securing strategic exploration agreements and MOUs in the Mediterranean, Africa and the Middle East are examples of the strong set of opportunities we have for the future. We're focused on executing with excellence in the near term, meeting or exceeding our guidance through the end of the decade and creating even more value in the decades that follow. Consistent with our long-standing financial priorities, we intend to reward our shareholders today, tomorrow and long into the future. I'll now hand it over to Jeanine.

transcript.speaker: Jeanine Wai
transcript.title: Head of Investor Relations
transcript.content: All right. Thank you, Eimear. This concludes our prepared remarks. Additional guidance can be found in the appendix to this presentation as well as on the slides and other information posted on chevron.com. We're now ready to take your questions. Katie, please open the lines.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: Our first question comes from Devin McDermott with Morgan Stanley.

transcript.speaker: Devin McDermott
transcript.title: Analyst (Morgan Stanley)
transcript.content: So Mike, Eimear, the goals you laid out with the corporate reorganization plan last year was more than just cost. It was also to support best-in-class operations. And I think the strong results this quarter clearly show that's paying off. So on the theme of operations, I wanted to start on TCO, which looks like it was one of the key drivers of higher production quarter-over-quarter. I was wondering if you could talk about performance there. Any learnings as far as it relates to quantifying or derisking the debottlenecking opportunity. And while we're on the topic, Mike, maybe you can just address the current situation at the CPC pipeline and any levers that Chevron has to mitigate any disruption there?

transcript.speaker: Michael Wirth
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Sure, Devin. Thanks for the comments about our reorganization. And you're right. It wasn't just about efficiency. It was also about performance. I'll speak to TCO performance and the pipeline. And Eimear, maybe you can cover the debottlenecking question. It was a strong quarter. You'll see in the production waterfall, we're up 170,000 barrels a day versus first quarter, really stellar operating performance in the second quarter. Each month was among the highest months we've ever seen at TCO. The affiliate distributions in the quarter of roughly $3 billion, most of that is coming from TCO and I want to affirm our $6 billion guidance at $70 Brent; obviously, we're likely to have a higher number for Brent this year, which would translate into even higher affiliate distributions. The team has been working incredibly hard on recovering from some of the first quarter issues. But really the most exciting thing is the ability to optimize across the entire field now. The low-pressure production performance of the field has been strong and through this integrated control center we take each generation of topside facilities and look at the way to best optimize those, not only individually, but collectively across the capabilities we have in all of the kit. The pipeline question: you've seen the media reports; there has been some activity in the Black Sea related to the Ukraine-Russia conflict that, over the last number of quarters, has intermittently had some impact on activity in and around overseas. I can tell you that today both of our SPMs are in service there. The third SPM has been down for a while, undergoing some refurbishment activities, and will be available here in the third quarter. So all three will be available later in the third quarter. The pipeline is flowing — we've been loading ships this week. Mitigation is the usual things: we can ship some across the Caspian; we can ship some on rail; we've got storage that we can use to buffer some of these ups and downs. But as you know, CPC is the primary route to market for that production for us and others on the pipeline. We're clearly a big shipper on it, but not the only shipper. We work with governments in the region, the U.S. government, the Kazakh government and other governments to be sure that pipeline stays flowing. It's critical to the world at a time when we need the energy. Eimear, maybe you can talk specifically about the debottlenecking of FGP and the third-generation plant.

transcript.speaker: Eimear Bonner
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Sure. So Devin, the debottlenecking efforts, as Mike said, are focused on the third-generation plant that we started up last year. Its original oil capacity is 260,000 barrels of oil per day. The teams conducted a turnaround in the fourth quarter of 2025, and during the turnaround they changed out some internals in a major column in that system. It was a very low capital modification. Since the fourth quarter last year, they have been testing the performance of that unit and its interaction with the rest of the utilities in the system in 3GP very extensively, testing different operating conditions. We are very comfortable to say today that we have successfully increased the nameplate oil capacity of 3GP from the original 260,000 barrels of oil per day to 320,000 barrels of oil per day. What that means for the overall total field processing capacity is that it now takes the total field processing capacity to slightly above 1 million barrels of oil per day. We're really encouraged by that. I'm confident that we can sustain that level of performance. The efforts by the team are consistent with our track record of looking for the technical limits in plant and increasing the capacity. They'll continue to focus on safely and reliably optimizing the plant and the production, optimizing through the integrated operations center from the reservoir through to the market. So we're really, really pleased with that.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We'll go next to Neil Mehta with Goldman Sachs.

transcript.speaker: Neil Mehta
transcript.title: Analyst (Goldman Sachs)
transcript.content: Yes. Thanks, Mike and Eimear. I just want to spend some time on the shale and tight part of the portfolio. And Mike, maybe you can give us how you're thinking about the different components there. The 25% less CapEx per barrel oil equivalent in '26 compared to last year is a good data point. It sounds like capital efficiency is moving in the right direction. Spend a little bit of time in the Bakken as you evaluate whether this is core or noncore and then spend some time in Vaca Muerta. Maybe a quick tour around the world would be great on shale and tight.

transcript.speaker: Michael Wirth
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Okay. Let me give you a couple of comments, and then I'll have Eimear talk about capital efficiency in the Permian in particular. We're producing on the order of 1.7 million barrels a day out of our shale and tight portfolio. One of the things I'm really pleased with in the new operating model is we brought all these assets together under common management. Previously, we had them reporting geographically, and we attempted to coordinate across those assets, but it's not the same as having one organization responsible for operating all of them and applying technology to all of them to optimize activity across the entire shale and tight portfolio. As you know, we've got multiple large assets in there: 1 million barrels a day in the Permian, 400,000 in the DJ, 200,000 in the Bakken. Argentina is smaller than that but growing. Out of the largest piece, the U.S. piece, we're working at plateau to generate free cash flow, which is the lesson the industry learned over the prior decade when it generated no free cash flow and all the cash went back into growth. At the scale we operate at now, we could grow these assets further, particularly in the Permian, if we chose, but we are working for efficiency, productivity and to generate free cash out of them. In the Bakken, we're getting to know the asset better. The person who runs all of our shale and tight came from Hess and is very familiar with the Bakken. I cited some of the things we're doing there differently already in terms of lateral length and drilling efficiencies: same production with one fewer rig. So we're getting to know that asset better as was the case with the DJ when we integrated it. Often the things you don't know, you can't underestimate. We like what we see in the Bakken. We've got to sort through the midstream thing that we get asked about on every one of these calls, and we'll let you know as we've got our thinking and plans together for that. It's been great to see the benefits across the entire portfolio that we've been able to drive by bringing them under common management. One of those benefits is continued capital efficiencies; just when you think there won't be much more and you might have climbed the improvement curve and started to level out, we continue to be surprised that there is more there. I think some of that is a result of being able to really focus on the performance of these assets as opposed to being driven by growth. Eimear, maybe you can talk a little bit more about the capital efficiency, particularly.

transcript.speaker: Eimear Bonner
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Yes. Thanks, Mike. The Permian has been operating for the last five quarters at over 1 million barrels per day, so they are seeing huge efficiencies with this focus on sweating the assets, not growing production, but growing free cash flow. Our capital is now expected to be below $3.5 billion this year, which is a 25% improvement in capital efficiency versus 2025. It's one of the reasons why we feel confident today to say that we expect to finish the year at the low end of our capital budget range of $18 billion to $19 billion. Maybe a few examples: we've talked before about drilling efficiencies and completion efficiencies. The Permian is also seeing the highest reliability it's seen since 2024. There are a lot of new initiatives, including optimizing artificial lift, real-time facility optimization, and a new approach to operations and maintenance through an asset tiering lens. All of those things are delivering really stellar reliability at surface as well as the drilling and completion efficiencies we've discussed before. We're really encouraged by what we've achieved. By bringing all of the shale and tight assets together to run them as one, we couldn't have done it without that integration because they're all learning from each other.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We'll take our next question from John Royall with Piper Sandler.

transcript.speaker: John Royall
transcript.title: Analyst (Piper Sandler)
transcript.content: So my question is on the power business, and I appreciate the update and the detail on Kilby. My question is more about how you view the long term for Chevron in the power business. It sounds to me from Jeff's commentary that you're uniquely positioned to serve this market and you mentioned potential future projects beyond Kilby. Can you talk about how much power could contribute to your business mix longer term? And how should we think about how it fits into the next decade plus of Chevron's growth story?

transcript.speaker: Jeff Gustavson
transcript.title: President, New Energy
transcript.content: Yes, John. Thanks for the question. We're very happy with the milestone we achieved in June with Microsoft — a high-quality customer and a 20-year firm PPA. It serves more than just that project. We see larger business potential here. Kilby is a good proof point: it demonstrates durable customer demand and that the behind-the-meter power model works for customers. It also shows that we bring differentiated capabilities to this market. I spoke about the structural shift in power demand where demand far exceeds supply. The grid cannot keep up with demand from hyperscalers and others, and we see that persisting for years. Our capabilities are deep: our large natural gas portfolio, experience in natural gas markets across the country, behind-the-meter power experience around the world in remote areas where you don't have grid options, and the requirement for very high reliability. Our complex project development and execution capabilities are important because these are very large-scale projects. Our customer and partner relationships and stakeholder engagement are also critical. Turbine availability is tight. We have deep relationships with GE Vernova and other manufacturers and are already talking to them. I think the Kilby announcement strengthens our position in these discussions and demonstrates we've converted an opportunity into an executable project. We'll pursue additional opportunities; we already have some discussions well underway with existing and new customers and partners. But we'll be disciplined as we move this forward and always focus on value over growth.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We'll take our next question from Doug Leggate with Wolfe Research.

transcript.speaker: Douglas George Blyth Leggate
transcript.title: Analyst (Wolfe Research)
transcript.content: Mike, I wonder if I could take a little bit of a longer term view. The U.S. has perhaps become — it's back in everybody's focus as a safe source of energy supply. And you paused your growth trajectory in the Permian some years ago to inflect to free cash flow. My question is, you've got a lot of things going on in the portfolio today. Guyana is inflecting to free cash flow. You've put a lot of stuff in the portfolio beyond your current plan. Where does the Permian fit? Could we see that go back to growth in the post-2030 outlook?

transcript.speaker: Michael Wirth
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Yes, Doug, thank you. Actually, it was just last year that we took the Permian to plateau. And if you look at it, it has continued to grow. I can have Jeanine follow up with you offline, but it actually has crept up and is still growing. The point here is we really want to focus the organization on efficiencies and productivity that Eimear talked about earlier, and we're seeing that in the Permian and in other assets as well. Could the Permian grow? Absolutely. But we've learned the lessons that at some point you want to see free cash out of these assets, and we're seeing that in significant quantums. We're working hard on technologies that can change the equation. We've talked in the past about advanced chemicals and AI; there's a lot of interesting work going on with simulation technologies and both incremental and potentially novel improvements to stimulation. We're leaving much of the hydrocarbons in the ground; there's a huge incentive to figure out how to unlock more. As we work these technology levers and see performance improvements, it changes your options: you can extend the plateau, create more value at plateau, or create more value through growth. We have thousands of well locations today; as we use technology to unlock horizons or benches that may not be economic using today's technology, that inventory increases. This is an advantaged asset given our long history there and our royalty position. We will work it to create value long into the future, and I expect we will unlock options over the coming years. On growth, there are three buckets I think about: enhanced opportunities such as our massive shale portfolio, Guyana, Eastern Med expansion projects, Argentina and West Africa; announced business development advancements in exploration, including new entries into Libya, Suriname and Namibia, and our continued leadership in the Gulf of America; and special situations we have some control over, like Venezuela and Iraq. In Iraq, due to circumstances with another party, there's opportunity at West Qurna 2. We're advancing negotiations on the TCO concession as well. Broadly, we have many growth options and will pursue the strongest while remaining capital disciplined. The Permian is one of many options for growth over the next decade.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We'll take our next question from Arun Jayaram with JPMorgan.

transcript.speaker: Arun Jayaram
transcript.title: Analyst (JPMorgan)
transcript.content: Mike, I wanted to get your perspective on Iraq. You look to be close to an entry to operate West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah. I'd love to see how you think that this Iraqi opportunity could compete for capital in your portfolio, how you view overall commercial terms, cost of supply and how you think about managing some of the aboveground risk?

transcript.speaker: Michael Wirth
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Sure. Obviously, potentially huge resources: third-party data on West Qurna 2 alone shows gross oil potential well into the billions of barrels; it's one of the largest oil fields in the world. We're advancing discussions to align on key commercial and economic principles for future contracts. It's a new form of contract. This month, we signed some follow-on agreements that significantly advanced the commercial discussions at both West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah. We see encouraging signs from the Iraqi government. The terms look like they will be competitive within our portfolio, but we still have work to do to finalize all the details. There's a cross-border pipeline concept that would allow alternative routes to market north through Iraq and potentially either through Syria or Turkey or perhaps both to get to the Mediterranean. We've got a framework to evaluate that and have talked to a number of interested parties who would participate; we would have a share, but many others would as well. All this needs final agreements, but it's advancing at pace. The Prime Minister has been personally engaged and very supportive, and we appreciate that leadership. We'll continue discussions in the coming months, and you'll hear about any final determinations when they occur.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We will take our next question from Steve Richardson with Evercore.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Richardson
transcript.title: Analyst (Evercore)
transcript.content: This is probably a good one for Eimear, but I'd love to just dig in a little bit on the achievement of the $3 billion of cost savings ahead of schedule and the 70% from efficiency gains. I was wondering if you could give us a sense of where you're seeing outperformance versus the plan? What have been some of the surprises? And what are some of the chunkier elements of what you're seeing as you're attacking these costs and your confidence level on sticking to these costs and not falling back into an inflationary trap?

transcript.speaker: Eimear Bonner
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Yes. We're absolutely thrilled to share that we achieved the $3 billion of structural cost reduction ahead of schedule. It's a testament to teams across the organization who have been relentlessly focused and achieved great results. Seventy percent of the results are associated with efficiency gains. We went through a massive restructuring and rewiring of the organization last year, and that is impacting results — about 35% of the 70% I referenced is related to that reorganization. The balance is associated with technology achievements, improvement initiatives across the organization and other measures. A few examples to demonstrate our confidence in sustainability: we centralized functions and created a technical center that allows centralized and standardized engineering work orders across the organization, and we're seeing results there. In maintenance reliability, the shale and tight business is running as one and has implemented predictive maintenance across assets, delivering results by detecting anomalies proactively and ensuring minimum production loss. Another example is turnaround optimization: tighter control of scope, prioritizing sequence and learning from each other. These changes are now built into the business, and we're very confident they'll continue to deliver. Costs always matter; we're never satisfied and never done. We have a strong culture focused on cost and continuous improvement.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We will take our next question from Biraj Borkhataria with RBC.

transcript.speaker: Biraj Borkhataria
transcript.title: Analyst (RBC)
transcript.content: I just wanted to follow up on CPC again. This is obviously a very significant pipeline that serves your asset and a number of your peers. I suspect there are a number of governments involved trying to solve this issue. But could you clarify if the CPC pipeline is closed for an extended period of time, how much of that roughly 1 million barrels a day of liquids could be evacuated by alternative routes? And related to that, in the Middle East there's a lot of discussion around building alternative evacuation to reduce the risk from the Strait of Hormuz. I'm wondering if anything incremental is being discussed here. I know the geography is challenging, but any thoughts would be helpful.

transcript.speaker: Michael Wirth
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Yes. Biraj, with CPC being the primary evacuation route, if it were to be shut down for an extended period, that would create issues for all shippers on that line. It services a number of projects in Kazakhstan, and some volumes come in from Russia as well. I mentioned our alternatives earlier: we've seen creativity used with CPC before. I don't think we've quantified the full alternative capacity, and I don't intend to here. You've seen creativity in the Strait of Hormuz over the years, and we've had to use some creativity at times with CPC too. The commitment to keeping CPC open from all parties that rely on it and governments that rely on it is very high, and I have a great degree of confidence that that commitment is real and that we will see CPC continue operating. I won't say it's never interrupted, but I don't think an intended, extended shutdown is a highly likely scenario. On your second question about the Strait, there are short-term actions like shuttling through the Strait and loading outside the Strait and medium-term ideas like the cross-border pipeline to the Mediterranean that I mentioned earlier. There are other similar ideas being advanced by others.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We will take our next question from James West with Melius Research.

transcript.speaker: James West
transcript.title: Analyst (Melius Research)
transcript.content: Wanted to — you very eloquently shifted a question on the Permian earlier to really walking around the world, demonstrating the optionality that you've put in place in various markets that are now turning into signed agreements and action. I wanted to dig in a little bit deeper on exploration in particular — Libya, Namibia, Greece — where are you most excited or where do you think you have the best upside potential? Where might the market be missing what you're up to?

transcript.speaker: Michael Wirth
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Thanks, James. This is the largest and highest-quality opportunity set we've had in years. We're building quality through choice. We increased our acreage by 35% over the last year and closed on 10 million net acres this year in South America, the Mediterranean and the Gulf of America primarily. Guyana remains a major focus, and there's still exploration potential there. West Africa — the deepwater of both Nigeria and Angola — is relatively underexplored, and I'm optimistic large basins with proven petroleum systems offer more opportunities. We intend to drill another well in Namibia where we've seen success. The Mediterranean is interesting; we've had success off Egypt and are a partner in a well where a working petroleum system has been established, which is important in exploration. The Middle East speaks for itself; in Iraq we have both operating fields and associated exploration prospects with large structures and strong analogs. We'll be disciplined in advancing the portfolio and will use new tools, including AI, which will change cycle times and our ability to see things previously unseen, and I expect it to improve outcomes. Over the last five years we've had multiple discoveries and successful appraisal wells in the Gulf of America, the Partitioned Zone and West Africa, and we intend to continue advancing this exploration portfolio. We'll be talking about this more in the years to come.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We will take our next question from Sam Margolin with Wells Fargo.

transcript.speaker: Sam Margolin
transcript.title: Analyst (Wells Fargo)
transcript.content: Maybe switching gears to natural gas: the gas market in Europe is exceptionally tight right now. Chevron in Australia typically has a volume ramp; Gorgon and Wheatstone typically have a little bit of a volume uplift in the second half of years starting in the third quarter. Can you just talk about your available LNG position right now and optimization opportunities to help solve this European shortage?

transcript.speaker: Michael Wirth
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: Yes, Sam. We do see some seasonality in Australia — cooler weather helps LNG facilities. Most of our Australian LNG is term-contracted with customers in Asia; we do have some spot cargoes, but that's a smaller portion of production. From West Africa, we've moved LNG into Europe more steadily on some shorter-term contracts and a fair amount of spot out of West Africa. We also have a growing position in North America with 4 million tons per annum that will come online over the next few years, and that position is primarily going into Europe. Australia is the longest route and is pretty well termed up; Asian spot markets have been strong. JKM and TTF have firmed, and I think demand in both North Asia and Europe is likely to remain strong over the next period. We'll make the best sales into each market and continue to operate at high reliability, and I'm pleased to say our Australian assets are operating reliably.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We will take our next question from Manav Gupta with UBS.

transcript.speaker: Manav Gupta
transcript.title: Analyst (UBS)
transcript.content: A lot of questions on CPC. I was hoping to talk a little bit about CPChem. There's a big jump in earnings. Global product inventory is depleted and the polyethylene side is also tight. Multiple global crackers are struggling, and you have a unique portfolio, mostly in North America. Could you talk about the leverage that CPChem has in this environment of elevated polyethylene margins?

transcript.speaker: Michael Wirth
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: I think you mostly answered the question yourself. CPChem's primary footprint is in North America, with some production in the Middle East, which is constrained right now given circumstances in the Strait. CPChem primarily cracks ethane in North America. Those margins have been under pressure over the last few years but have been buoyant in recent months as naphtha availability out of the Middle East has been constrained. Naphtha normally flows into North Asia and sets the price there. Ethane crackers are lower cost, so their margins tend to be better, and in an environment of production tightening, CPChem is advantaged. We'll see how long this tightness lasts; I can't predict when things in the Strait will settle down, but we're very pleased with CPChem's performance right now.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We will take our next question from Jean Ann Salisbury with Bank of America.

transcript.speaker: Jean Ann Salisbury
transcript.title: Analyst (Bank of America)
transcript.content: Can you discuss your decision to license your surfactant technology versus keeping it in-house? How did you view the pros and cons there? And how large could this revenue stream be?

transcript.speaker: Eimear Bonner
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Jean Ann, I'm happy to take this. We're excited about the decision. The rationale was to explore another pathway for innovation. Advanced chemicals are a big focus for improving recoveries across our shale and tight asset class. We have a lot of work underway deploying pilots and trying different chemicals, and partnering with a company that has manufacturing, distribution and pumping service capabilities allows us to co-innovate and accelerate scaling this technology with speed. We have many non-operated joint venture volumes, so having a partner allows us to offer this solution to NOJV partners; it's a win-win. We see this as a way to accelerate progress on improving shale and tight recovery across basins. On materiality, Mike noted the contribution from recoveries will likely be much larger than licensing revenue; licensing revenue will exist, but the application of the chemicals is the real opportunity.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We will take our next question from Betty Jiang with Barclays.

transcript.speaker: Wei Jiang
transcript.title: Analyst (Barclays)
transcript.content: Probably a question for Eimear on long-term CapEx. You mentioned earlier that Permian CapEx is falling below $3.5 billion and a lot of that is driven by capital efficiencies, which I imagine will put downward pressure on Permian CapEx going forward. At the same time, you have power folding in as well. Could you remind us what's driving the range for long-term CapEx and whether we could see that number trending lower as well?

transcript.speaker: Eimear Bonner
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Yes. In terms of the long-term range we shared at Investor Day, we provided a range of $18 billion to $21 billion. This year, our budget is $18 billion to $19 billion. That range represents the opportunities we have over the next five years. We had expected to have a power project within that capital range, and the Kilby project Jeff discussed is reflected in both the organic capital outlook and the affiliate capital outlook. At the end of the day, we'll remain capital disciplined. Mike talked about the growth options we're stacking globally, both in power and upstream. We believe that range gives us enough optionality for the projects on the table today.

transcript.speaker: Operator
transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We will take our next question from Nitin Kumar with Mizuho Securities.

transcript.speaker: Nitin Kumar
transcript.title: Analyst (Mizuho Securities)
transcript.content: I want to shift gears a bit to refining. Refining had a good quarter given the macro environment. Mike, I was wondering if you could talk about the outlook post the war: are you seeing any evidence of demand destruction as things remain tight, and what's your view on the cracks here?

transcript.speaker: Michael Wirth
transcript.title: Chairman and CEO
transcript.content: I'll be brief. Middle distillates are the tight spot right now. Initially it looked like jet; now it's diesel. European diesel demand was weaker in the second quarter, which I think kept global inventories from drawing further. That may not hold up into the third quarter. Restocking of heating oil ahead of winter, the Russian export ban, refinery outages in Russia and constraints in the Strait all add pressure. Mogas inventories are low as well. Products are tighter than crude globally, which is why cracks have widened. The question is when crude flows reestablish and when cracks come back in — hard to say. I expect upward pressure on product pricing into the third quarter and perhaps beyond. Demand destruction is not obvious at scale. China is a black box and is a big question for us, and other Asian markets that faced physical constraints may see short-term demand impacts. But longer-term structural demand destruction is hard to find evidence for today.

transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We will take our next question from Bob Brackett with Bernstein.

transcript.speaker: Bob Brackett
transcript.title: Analyst (Bernstein)
transcript.content: If I think about Project Kilby, you've talked about expected mid-teens returns, and that's really a ring fence around the take-or-pay and standing up that power generation. Are there additional opportunities to create value given you're sitting in a county with plenty of acres and wells? Is there additional add-on value potentially?

transcript.speaker: Jeff Gustavson
transcript.title: President, New Energy
transcript.content: Yes, Bob. There could be. There could be expansion potential on the Kilby site after the first phase and after we ramp up to 2.67 gigawatts. None of that has been agreed with Microsoft yet, but their demand needs continue to increase, and we'll work with them if expansion meets our return thresholds. I talked about scaling this business further; we don't see Kilby as a one-off. The macro demand environment is durable and the depth of our capabilities is differentiated. Microsoft saw that with Kilby, and others are interested in growth beyond this in West Texas and perhaps other parts of the U.S. We'll remain disciplined and stick to return thresholds. We'll provide more information as growth opportunities emerge.

transcript.title: Operator
transcript.content: We'll take our next question from Jason Gabelman with TD Cowen.

transcript.speaker: Jason Gabelman
transcript.title: Analyst (TD Cowen)
transcript.content: I wanted to ask on Venezuela. I imagine you're getting to the point where the amount they owe you is going to be fully repaid. When that point comes, do your contractual terms shift to the new fiscal framework they're developing, or is there something in place today you would fall under? More broadly, how are the contract negotiations going to unlock additional volumes and how do you think about incremental investment and production growth over the medium term?

transcript.speaker: Eimear Bonner
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Jason, on debt recovery, we are continuing to recover our debt and expect it to be fully recovered by early 2027. Today we are operating three joint ventures very successfully. We've grown production over the last few years from 40,000 to 250,000 barrels per day. With the existing model we have in place, we have grown production from those three JVs 15% over the last six months to 280,000 barrels of oil per day, and we anticipate being able to grow up to 50% between now and the end of 2028. Operationally, everything in Venezuela is going well and consistent with what we communicated. Regarding other opportunities, we've been in Venezuela for 100 years and stayed because of the potential in the country and the assets. We like the heavy oil assets there and have experience in this space. We're actively working with the government to look at other opportunities. We'll be disciplined; the terms we're discussing are confidential, but they must be competitive and compete in our portfolio for capital. We're encouraged by where we are with Venezuela on these additional opportunities.

transcript.content: Can you update us on your latest thoughts around future investment across Argentina in Vaca Muerta? I think you were down there in May, and we saw some reports around a large development potential. It's always been a large contributor to other shale and tight. Hoping you could update us on the potential here and what gives you the confidence now to push forward.

transcript.speaker: Eimear Bonner
transcript.title: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.content: Thanks, Phillip. We're really excited about the opportunity in Argentina. We have history there across three development areas where we are an operator or nonoperated partner. We are producing 80,000 barrels a day from Argentina with about a 70% to 75% oil cut, so we like the product slate from Vaca Muerta. We're leveraging lessons from our shale and tight organization, which now includes the Bakken, DJ and Permian, to deliver on growth we shared at Investor Day, aiming to grow threefold by 2035. The engagement you referenced was with the Minister of Economy; we discussed the rig framework that has recently been extended to oil and gas. We have applied for the El Trapial asset. This framework gives up to 30 years of fiscal stability with incentives like accelerated depreciation and tax incentives, which makes Argentina much more competitive as a growth option. We'll continue to be disciplined; no change in the near term, but there's a lot of opportunity to grow.
